web_evidence.title: Excerpt: ‘The Lovely Bones’
web_evidence.note: A sustained Chapter One excerpt, reproduced with Little, Brown's permission, begins with Susie identifying herself and recounting her murder and life through I/my narration.

web_evidence.title: The End of the Good Life: Literary Representations of Suburbia and the American Nightmare
web_evidence.note: University of Edinburgh scholarly analysis identifies Susie as the first-person narrator and describes her first-person omnipotent voice as carrying the remainder of the narrative while accessing other characters' thoughts.

web_evidence.title: Women Writing Trauma: How Female Writers Use Narrative Voice in Fiction to Represent the Effects of Trauma
web_evidence.note: A University of South Wales MPhil study classifies the deceased protagonist Susie as the novel's first-person omniscient and omnipresent narrator from the afterlife.

web_evidence.title: PW Talks with Alice Sebold
web_evidence.note: The contemporary author interview identifies murdered character Susie Salmon as the novel's narrator and discusses Sebold finding Susie's voice and placing her in heaven.

person_note: The controlling narrator is Susie Salmon, a participant who tells her own death and observes her family from heaven in first person. Numerous quotes independently expose her I/my voice, and the permissioned opening plus scholarly whole-book analyses agree. Third-person-looking passages about Ray or Ruth reflect Susie's unusual omniscient reach and do not establish a nonparticipating narrator. The second-person forms in q00952 are generalized or reader-directed within her first-person account, q00961 is attributed local material from Jack, and q00962 remains diagnostic because its dialogue is surrounded by Susie's first-person beats. The only scope limitation is that the authorized prose source covers the opening, but the whole-book scholarly sources resolve that limitation and reveal no sustained person alternation.
